text.text: Up until now, the role of dispositions in the psychosocial effects of adolescent instant messaging (IM) remains inconclusive.

While the straightforward rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer hypotheses do not allow for nuances about the individual-specific (dis)advantages of offline and online interactions, the literature on the dispositional tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation shows a more complex picture.

In this ecological momentary study (one week, 8 assessments/day), we adopted the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer framework to test the social and psychological effects of IM with regard to the dispositional tendencies for co-rumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing in 181 Belgian adolescents (n = 181; Mage = 15.04; 63% women).
Adolescents with a higher tendency for co-dampening reported lower mean levels of momentary positive affect.
Individuals with a clear tendency for co-enhancing experienced, on average, higher momentary IM emotional support.
Regarding the tendency for co-rumination, no significant differences were found.
Notably, (dis)advantageous social effects did not go together with similar psychological effects.
Unexpectedly, IM behaviors (e.g., IM negative social exchange) were, regardless of the studied outcome and the level of analysis, systematically significant.
Overall, this study endorses the importance of the abovementioned dispositional tendencies.
Yet, their value was more limited than the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses predicted.

text.text: Consistent with the aforementioned recommendations, the study of how adolescents generally tend to regulate their emotions in interaction with peers (i.e., interpersonal emotion regulation; IER; e.g., chatting with one's best friend about being chosen last for a group assignment) shows potential in the investigation of the social and psychological effects of -by definition interactive -instant messaging conversations with peers.
Indeed, the most well-known type of interpersonal emotion regulation, co-rumination (i.e., rehashing problems with a confidant), does not uniformly fit the "rich vs poor" typology.

Although the tendency to co-ruminate is associated with smaller support networks and fewer social skills (Tompkins et al., 2011), co-ruminating adolescents report, both concurrently and prospectively, close dyadic friendship bonds (e.g., Rose et al., 2007).

text.text: This EMA study challenges the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypothesis from an IERperspective.

By focusing on the dispositional tendency for co-rumination, co-dampening and coenhancing, we address the hypotheses' conceptual gap that the effects of instant messaging uniformly depend on the level of the dispositional traits.
We will tackle two complementary research questions series, focusing on the social and psychological effects of instant messaging in everyday life respectively.
For this purpose, we study associations with regard to IM conversations with friends or close friends.

Striving to approximate reality as close as possible, we incorporate both time-varying positive (i.e., IM emotional support) and negative aspects of instant messaging (i.e., IM negative social exchange; e.g., the perception of being distracted by the messages) in the analyses.

Regarding the social effects of IM, we will first explore whether the dispositional tendency for co-rumination, co-dampening and co-enhancing predicts differences in the mean level of momentary IM emotional support (i.e., RQ 1A).
That is, do adolescents who tend to co-ruminate, co-dampen and co-enhance with their best friend feel generally more connected during IM conversations?

Furthermore, we will exploratively determine if the dispositional tendency for co-rumination, codampening and co-enhancing alters the strength of the within-person association between momentary IM negative social exchange and momentary IM emotional support (i.e., RQ 1B).

For example, if we find that "when the IM conversation proceeds with less social friction than usual, adolescents feel more emotionally supported in the chat", does this association becomes stronger or weaker for individuals with higher scores on the dispositional tendencies?
For the psychological effects of IM, the outcomes (a) depressive feelings and (b) positive affect will be studied.

Based on the philosophy of the rich-getricher and the poor-get-richer hypothesis, we will investigate if the dispositional tendency for corumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing predicts differences in the mean level of momentary mental health (i.e., RQ 2A).

Secondly, we intend to discover whether the dispositional tendency for corumination, co-dampening and co-enhancing alters the strength of the within-person association between momentary IM emotional support and momentary mental health (i.e., RQ 2B).

In line with the abovementioned literature, we expect an advantageous social effect and partially (dis)advantageous psychological effects (i.c., increased positive affect, increased depressive feelings) for individuals with a higher tendency for co-rumination.
Moreover, for adolescents with a higher tendency for co-dampening, an unfavorable social effect and insignificant psychological effects are anticipated.
With regard to the tendency for co-enhancing, we expect beneficial social and psychological effects.
Regarding the explorative questions, no hypotheses were formulated.

text.text: The data collection of this project was directed at the general adolescent population.
Adolescents could take part as long as they attended courses in secondary school.
No other selection criteria were applied.
Interested individuals and their parents were invited to an online information session in which the procedure and the EMA questions were addressed in detail.
In line with institutional ethical approval (1432023000129), parents and adolescents signed an informed consent respectively informed assent.
After the session, adolescents were requested to fill in a baseline questionnaire with trait measures.

Regarding the psychological outcomes of IM conversations with (close) friends, a series of six RDSEM models were studied: three models with depressive feelings and three models with positive affect as main outcome.
Each of these models focused on one dispositional tendency.

Confronted with inconsistencies surrounding online interactions in adolescence, this study applied the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer frameworks (Kraut et al., 2002) in an IM context while incorporating alternately the trait-like tendencies for co-rumination, co-dampening, and co-enhancing.

text.text: Although none of the three IER-strategies could be clearly labeled as "rich" or "poor" according to the scientific literature about offline interactions, this study showed a more straightforward picture in which adolescents with a tendency for co-enhancing became unequivocally richer through IM conversations and individuals with a tendency for co-dampening became poorer.

Yet, contrasting with the predictions of the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses, the social and psychological effects of the dispositional tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation did not go hand-in-hand.
Below, the detailed social and psychological outcomes for each IER-tendency are explored.
Apart from the effects related to sex, all co-rumination models showed no relevant significant results.

Hence, adolescents with a higher tendency for co-rumination did not report better or worse social and psychological average momentary effects after accounting for positive or negative timevarying aspects of IM and the time-dynamics of the models.
Relatedly, the dispositional tendency for co-rumination did not alter the strength of the studied associations.
Building on the literature about co-rumination as a depositional tendency and a behavior, these findings are surprising.

Adolescents with a tendency for co-dampening might benefit from "guidelines" how they could deal with positive experiences more neutrally, without actively diminishing positive emotions.
Reversibly, friends might profit from tips on how to react in a supportive yet nonreinforcing way on the dampening of their friend.

In this study, we explored the rich-get-richer and the poor-get-richer hypotheses from the nontraditional angle of the tendency for interpersonal emotion regulation.
Both social and psychological outcomes were studied while taking adolescents' instant messaging conversations with friends and close friends into account.

Although all three tendencies for interpersonal emotion regulation could not be easily classified as "rich" or "poor" based on the literature about their offline life, our study showed a clear-cut view.
Individuals with a higher tendency for co-dampening had a lower mean level of momentary positive affect, which points to an unambiguous "get poorer"-effect.
In addition, the tendency for co-enhancing predicted differences in the mean level of IM emotional support (i.e., higher), a clear "get richer"-effect.
For the tendency for co-rumination, we unexpectedly did not find significant results.
Contrary to the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer framework, the dispositional tendencies did not significantly affect both the social and psychological outcomes at the same time.
Additionally, all explorative cross-level interactions were insignificant.
Third, although not in line with the rich-get-richer and poor-get-richer hypotheses, IM behavior consistently proved to be a predictor of all studied outcomes.
Overall, this study endorses the socially beneficial value of a tendency for coenhancing and the psychological disadvantage related to a tendency for co-dampening.
Moreover, more attention should be devoted to possible (IM) behavioral determinants of psychosocial outcomes that fluctuate throughout time.
Furthermore, we measured the tendency for co-rumination, co-dampening and co-enhancing in a very specific way.
Firstly, all three tendencies were measured in relation to one's best same-sex friend.
This means that these tendencies are in essence interactive.
Yet, these tendencies were only assessed from a subjective self-report perspective.
Reciprocal assessments that merge information provided by both friends and therefore allow to calculate more objective (latent) trait scores, should be further explored in the future.
Secondly, the time-varying constructs of this study (e.g., IM emotional support) were measured while referring to the last IM conversation with one's close friends and friends.
Consequently, these interactions do not necessary involve one-on-one contacts with one's best friend.

Relevantly, IM conversations with regular friends or group chats in which several people are involved might be less intimate (Cooney et al., 2020) and might thus engender less interpersonal emotion regulation.
